title: Myth vs Fact: AI faked the CEO's voice - inside the alleged $129M deepfake fraud
description:
On November 5, 2026, US federal prosecutors in New York (Southern District of New York) charged three men over an alleged scheme that used AI to impersonate company CEOs and lawyers. Prosecutors say the group took about $129 million from companies. These are allegations; none of the three has been convicted in this case.

Myth 1: "I'd recognise my own CEO's voice."
Fact: prosecutors say the group used AI to mimic the CEO's voice, and sometimes the CEO's image, on phone and video calls with accounting staff. In December 2024 the FBI warned that criminals use AI-generated video to pose as company executives in real-time video chats (PSA I-120324-PSA).

Myth 2: "Only small, careless firms fall for this."
Fact: victims named in court papers include hospital systems in Missouri and California, a bank in Rhode Island, a UK financial technology company, a Massachusetts mutual fund company and a Florida pet food company. Prosecutors say thousands of companies were targeted over more than a year and a half.

Myth 3: "A lawyer on the deal makes it legit."
Fact: the lawyers were fake too. As alleged: an email from the "CEO" about a confidential deal, an AI call in the CEO's voice, a hand-off to an impersonated attorney at a major law firm, then wires to accounts abroad and conversion to cryptocurrency. Prosecutors say one defendant used a handwritten script titled "Lawyer Call".

Analyst note (Securidge analysis): a familiar voice is no longer proof of identity. Your payment process has to catch what your ears cannot.

Before any urgent transfer
1. Hang up and call back on a number you already know (FBI advice).
2. Require a second approver for large payments.
3. Agree a code word with your team and your family (FBI advice).
4. Treat "keep this secret" as a red flag.

Sources
